stories.notes: Story has no acceptance criteria and null spec. Live preview across three platforms (GO, UP, MX) is complex and critical — involves real-time rendering, state sync, and iframe/content security concerns. openspec runs first to elaborate AC and propose platform splits; speckit then hardens with testability, security, and edge-case coverage.

agentContributions.notes: Story requests a new live-preview capability for CMS content editors. No existing preview mechanism exists in the codebase — useContent is the single content-fetching hook (236+ callers) and is the natural attachment point. Contentstack is an unreachable external service at test time, so VCs are scoped to our side of that boundary.

Openspec produced an empty AC list with a useful note identifying useContent as the natural attachment point and Contentstack as unreachable at test time. I built the full criteria set from the story title, description, file paths, and openspec's note. Criteria cover: happy-path preview delivery (AC-1, AC-2), session lifecycle (AC-3, AC-4), degradation (AC-5, AC-13), backward compatibility (AC-6, AC-11), malformed data (AC-7, AC-10), rapid updates/out-of-order delivery (AC-8, AC-15), security/no data leakage (AC-9), component-specific behavior for ContentstackLink (AC-12) and contentCard (AC-14). IMPORTANT CAVEAT: I could not read the source files (useContent.ts, ContentstackContext.tsx, contentCard.ts, ContentstackLink.tsx). My criteria are inferred from standard Contentstack live-preview patterns and the file paths provided. Specific field names, hook signatures, or content type shapes may need adjustment once the actual source is reviewed. If useContent has a shape incompatible with these criteria (e.g., it doesn't return content objects but triggers side effects), AC-6 and AC-11 would need revision.

coordinatorReview.reviewNotes: Both agents contributed but value was lopsided and carried significant risk. Openspec identified the correct codebase attachment point (useContent hook, 236+ callers) and the testability boundary (Contentstack unreachable at test time), which is useful context — but it produced an empty AC list, failing its primary elaboration responsibility. Speckit then built the entire 15-AC criteria set from scratch based on inference from the story title and standard Contentstack patterns, explicitly stating it could not read the actual source files (useContent.ts, ContentstackContext.tsx, contentCard.ts, ContentstackLink.tsx). The resulting ACs cover a broad surface (happy-path, session lifecycle, degradation, backward compatibility, malformed data, rapid updates, security, component-specific behavior) but are built on assumptions about hook signatures, field names, and content type shapes that may not match the real codebase. Speckit's own caveat flags that AC-6 and AC-11 would need revision if useContent has an incompatible shape. The collaborative pipeline broke down: openspec provided no elaborated output for speckit to harden, so speckit had to reconstruct requirements from scratch without source access. Human review is needed to validate the inferred ACs against actual source code before implementation.
